--- title: "13 — Tracking a drifting DARM parameter" description: "Tracking DARM calibration parameters that drift: κ(t), the SRC detuning δ(t), then several at once, with Lataire–Pintelon fits inside Cramér–Rao bands." image: thumbnails/13.svg image-alt: "A drifting calibration parameter tracked over time inside its Cramer-Rao band." categories: [calibration, closed-loop, DARM, time-varying] freeze: true --- ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## Contents - Why a drifting plant is a system-ID problem rather than a re-measurement chore. - Recovering a time-varying actuation strength κ(t) from leakage-free snapshots, with a measured CRB. - Tracking the SRC detuning δ(t) — the physics the coupled plant adds, where the cavity pole splits into a complex pair — from the Pcal FRF, independent of the κ drift. - Tracking several parameters drifting at once, at random (a joint fit), and reading off from the correlation matrix which drifts are hard to separate. - Establishing that each drift is resolvable with a computed bound rather than by inspection. ::: The [DARM calibration page](08-darm-calibration.qmd) recovers the loop's sensing, actuation, and response at one instant. The reason DARM calibration is the slowest recurring LIGO measurement is that those parameters drift — the optical gain, the coupled-cavity pole, and the actuation strengths wander over minutes to hours, so the calibration is re-measured again and again. This page treats that drift as a slowly time-varying system to identify, not a nuisance to average away. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## The plant and the scope This runs on the coupled DARM plant — the M0-damped reduced-QUAD hierarchical actuation (M0 / PUM / ESD) with coupled detuned-cavity sensing, where the SRC detuning splits the cavity pole into a complex pair (the same twin as [example 08](08-darm-calibration.qmd)). The build-up is in three steps: a single actuation strength κ(t) on a smooth curve, then the SRC detuning δ(t), then the realistic case — several parameters drifting at once, at random, recovered jointly. Still deferred: a Gaussian-process wander with a measured drift spectrum, all seven TDCFs together, and the one-shot (rather than two-step) Lataire–Pintelon fit. Rendered with `freeze: true`. ::: ::: {#86b38127 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Setup — import the presentation glue"} import sys, pathlib _p = pathlib.Path.cwd() for _c in [_p, *_p.parents]: if (_c / "docs" / "darm_tv_demo.py").exists() and str(_c / "docs") not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c / "docs")) if (_c / "darm_tv_demo.py").exists() and str(_c) not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c)) import numpy as np import darm_tv_demo as dd from IPython.display import display ``` ::: ## The idea: locally stationary snapshots The plant drifts far more slowly than one measurement record (an hour-scale drift versus a ~16 s record), so within any single record it is locally stationary — the Pintelon–Schoukens picture of a linear model around a slowly-moving operating point. That licenses a two-step estimator: 1. **Snapshot.** At a sequence of times, take one leakage-free periodic-multisine measurement and recover the instantaneous actuation strength with Pcal as the ruler. Because the sensing `C` cancels in the stage-to-Pcal ratio, each snapshot is independent of sensing drift and carries its own per-estimate σ. 2. **Basis fit.** Fit `κ(t) = Σ cₖ bₖ(t)` in a time-basis (Legendre) to the snapshot series by weighted least squares — a Lataire–Pintelon basis expansion in two-step form. The coefficient covariance is the Cramér–Rao bound on the drift curve κ(t) and its rate. The drifted stage is the ESD (TST) — the one whose strength wanders in an interferometer, as charge builds on the reaction mass — with a 5 %, hour-scale profile, on the coupled reduced-quad plant (the ruler `H_stage/H_pcal = κ_i·D_i·N_i` recovers κ through the M0-damped compliance and the nested-offload distribution). ::: {#8b08acf6 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Run the campaign — snapshot the drift, fit κ(t)"} c = dd.campaign(seed=777) ``` ::: ## Tracking the drift The injected truth, the per-record snapshots with their error bars, and the recovered κ(t) with its CRB band: ::: {#cell-fig-tv-kappa .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="κ(t): injected truth, snapshots ± σ, LP fit ± CRB"} dd.drift_fig(c) ``` ::: {#fig-tv-kappa .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` A drifting actuation strength κ(t): the injected truth, the per-snapshot estimates with their ±σ, and the Lataire–Pintelon fit with its Cramér–Rao band. ::: ::: The fit passes through the snapshots and follows the injected drift: a 5 % excursion resolved, even though each single snapshot pins κ only to about a percent. ## Calibration of the tracking uncertainty A curve through points is not sufficient; the curve has to carry its own uncertainty. The recovery residual (recovered − truth) stays inside the ±σ Cramér–Rao band — the error bar neither collapses (which would be fabricated confidence) nor balloons (which would be uselessly conservative): ::: {#cell-fig-tv-tracking .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Tracking error vs the CRB band"} dd.tracking_error_fig(c) ``` ::: {#fig-tv-tracking .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Tracking error against the Cramér–Rao band. The error stays inside the band, so the reported uncertainty is the realised one. ::: ::: ## The feasibility gate: is the drift resolvable? Before calling a drift trackable or buried in noise, compute the bound. The tracking σ from the fit is far below the injected drift amplitude, so the drift is resolved rather than noise, and the local-stationarity approximation costs a fraction of a percent, well under the per-snapshot error: ::: {#00f0af92 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Resolvability — a computed bound, not an eyeball"} display(dd.resolvability_table(c)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Feasibility gate — the injected drift is resolvable (a computed bound, not an eyeball)** | feasibility quantity | value | note | | --- | --- | --- | | injected drift amplitude | 0.0500 | 5% of κ | | per-snapshot σ_κ (median) | 0.0011 | 0.11% of κ | | tracking σ_κ (LP fit, median) | 0.0006 | 0.06% of κ | | resolve ratio = amp / tracking σ | 88× | ≫ 1 ⇒ drift resolved, not noise | | local-stationarity error | 0.22% | record ÷ drift timescale — the approximation cost | ::: ::: The resolve ratio is a controlled variable, not a limit: more periods per snapshot, more snapshots, or a stronger drive all reduce it — the same Fisher levers as everywhere else in the pipeline. ## A drifting SRC detuning δ(t) The coupled plant admits a drift the single-pole twin could not represent: the SRC detuning δ. As the SRC error point wanders around its slightly-detuned operating point, the cavity pole moves — splitting toward a complex pair — and the sensing shape changes with it. δ is a sensing parameter, so it does not cancel in the κ ruler; it is instead recovered from the Pcal FRF shape (`C_meas = H_pcal·(1+G)`), which makes the δ snapshot independent of the κ drift, so the two compose into a joint κ(t), δ(t) picture. δ is drifted by 5 % around a 5° operating point: ::: {#cell-fig-tv-delta .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Snapshot the drifting SRC detuning δ(t) from the Pcal FRF, fit δ(t)"} cd = dd.campaign_delta(seed=778) dd.delta_drift_fig(cd) ``` ::: {#fig-tv-delta .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` A drifting SRC detuning δ(t) snapshotted from the Pcal FRF and fitted, recovered independently of the κ drift. ::: ::: ::: {#b7b50fc4 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="δ(t) resolvability — a computed bound"} display(dd.delta_resolvability_table(cd)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **SRC-detuning drift is resolvable — δ tracked from the Pcal FRF, independent of the κ drift (the two snapshots compose).** | feasibility quantity | value | note | | --- | --- | --- | | injected drift amplitude | 0.2500° | 5% of δ | | per-snapshot σ_δ (median) | 0.0017° | 0.03% of δ | | tracking σ_δ (LP fit, median) | 0.0009° | 0.02% of δ | | resolve ratio = amp / tracking σ | 288× | ≫ 1 ⇒ drift resolved, not noise | | local-stationarity error | 0.22% | record ÷ drift timescale | ::: ::: The detuning is recovered to a hundredth of a degree per snapshot — the coupled-cavity split leaves a strong high-frequency signature in `C`, so δ is well-identified even at this small detuning. Note the separation of concerns: κ comes from the stage/Pcal ratio (independent of sensing drift), δ from the Pcal shape (independent of actuation drift), so a real interferometer's simultaneous κ- and δ-drift are tracked by two independent snapshots on the same records. ## Round 2: several parameters drifting at once, at random The two sections above each drift one parameter along a smooth curve. Both are simplifications: several calibration numbers wander simultaneously, and the wander is random (a meandering walk) rather than a sine. This section does both — the optical gain `κ_C`, the SRC detuning `δ`, and the ESD strength `κ_ESD` all drift together as random (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck) walks, and each record is fit for all three at once. A joint fit is necessary because the parameters are not independent: a wobble in one can present as a wobble in another, and only a joint fit — with the Pcal record pinning the sensing and each stage record pinning its own strength — separates them. ::: {#cell-fig-tv-joint .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Three random drifts at once, recovered in one joint fit per record"} cj = dd.campaign_joint(seed=2024) dd.joint_drift_fig(cj) ``` ::: {#fig-tv-joint .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Three parameters drifting at random simultaneously, each recovered by one joint fit per record. ::: ::: All three random wanders are followed within their error bars. The correlation matrix of a single snapshot shows how well they separate: ::: {#cell-fig-tv-corr .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Which drifts are hard to tell apart"} dd.joint_corr_fig(cj) ``` ::: {#fig-tv-corr .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Correlation matrix of the joint drift fit. Off-diagonal magnitude is how hard two drifts are to tell apart from this measurement. ::: ::: `δ` separates cleanly from the two gains (near-zero correlation) — it lives in the sensing shape, which the amplitudes do not touch. `κ_C` (optical gain) and `κ_ESD` (test-mass drive) are strongly anti-correlated: both scale the ESD line, so the loop shape alone cannot distinguish an optical-gain change from an actuation change — the Pcal absolute reference breaks the tie, which is why Pcal is the fiducial in a real calibration. The joint fit reports that degeneracy rather than concealing it in a one-at-a-time recovery. ## Designing the drive: a few optimal lines, not broadband The rounds above inject a broadband multisine — power in every bin — which is neither how a real calibration drives the interferometer nor what optimal excitation calls for. The plant is one system (the opto-mechanical DARM sensing `C` plus the quad suspension) with one joint parameter vector, and it is read out by a few always-on calibration lines. The question is where to place those lines. Given a prior on how much each parameter drifts, a handful of lines — Pcal lines plus one per in-band stage — are placed and weighted to minimise the joint estimator variance on the drifts (a Bayesian A-optimal design), under the real force budgets: the Pcal's ±200 mW photon-calibrator range, and each suspension stage capped at the same displacement ruler. Every line informs every parameter — a suspension line passes through `C` and `1/(1+G)` so it carries sensing information, and the Pcal ruler, compared against a suspension line, carries actuation information — so the design works on the coupled Fisher matrix, not two separate problems. ::: {#cell-fig-tv-design .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Design the A-optimal cal-line roster and score it against a broadband drive"} dc = dd.design_campaign() dd.design_fig(dc) ``` ::: {#fig-tv-design .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` The A-optimal calibration-line roster designed for these parameters, scored against a broadband drive of equal power. ::: ::: ::: {#684d710a .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Per-parameter drift prior, snapshot σ, and the resolvability margin"} display(dd.design_table(dc)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **A-optimal designed drive: joint cost 0.003 vs 0.007 for a broadband multisine of the same budget. The cost is Σ (snapshot σ / drift prior)² = Σ 1/margin² (lower = better; < 1 per parameter ⇒ its drift is resolved). Every drift here is resolved (margin > 1). κ_C's prior is measured (Sun 2020); the others are representative placeholders.** | parameter | drift prior (1σ) | snapshot σ | margin | prior source | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | κ_C (optical gain) | 2.0% | 5.06e-05 | 396× | Sun 2020 (measured 1–2 %) | | δ (SRC detuning) | 1.15° | 1.13e-03 | 18× | representative placeholder | | κ_PUM (L2 drive) | 2.0% | 5.34e-05 | 374× | representative placeholder | | κ_ESD (test-mass drive) | 2.0% | 1.35e-04 | 148× | representative placeholder | ::: ::: A handful of designed lines reaches a lower joint cost than a broadband multisine that spends the same budget over ~six times as many lines — the drive is placed where each parameter is informative, rather than spread across the band, much of which is the seismic wall or a stage's dead zone. Injecting exactly this roster on the twin and reading it back leakage-free recovers the drifting parameters: ::: {#cell-fig-tv-lines .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Track the joint set from the designed cal-line readout (not broadband)"} tc = dd.tracked_lines_campaign() dd.tracked_lines_fig(tc) ``` ::: {#fig-tv-lines .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` The joint parameter set tracked from the designed calibration-line readout rather than a broadband drive. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## What is grounded, and what the scope is The κ_C drift prior is measured (Sun et al. 2020: the optical gain varies 1–2 % over a run); the Pcal budget is real (±200 mW → `pcal_range_disp`); the O4 line frequencies are published (Wade et al. 2025, Fig. 4). The drift priors for `δ`, `κ_PUM`, `κ_ESD` are representative placeholders — the O3/O4 papers do not quantify them — and the per-stage force caps are derived by matching the Pcal ruler, since the papers give no per-stage line amplitude. The design tracks the identifiable joint set for this twin and the O4 floor: `κ_C`, `δ`, and the two in-band stages `κ_PUM`/`κ_ESD`. The other TDCFs are feasibility-gated rather than omitted: - **`κ_M0`** — the design frequency band runs down to 1 Hz (there is no arbitrary cap), and the placement uses the seismic wall extrapolated below 10 Hz (`darm_o4_asd_seismic`, ≈ f⁻⁷). With that floor the top mass is constrained from both sides: below ~10 Hz the seismic wall buries its line, and above ~10 Hz its own hierarchical offload rolls its DARM authority off as ≈ f⁻⁸. A leakage-free simulation confirms the line cannot be recovered anywhere in band, so `κ_M0` is not claimed here — it would require a sub-Hz line, where the detector has no sensitivity. (The analytic Fisher is optimistic for this offloaded stage; the simulation is the arbiter.) - **`f_cc`/`τ`** need a wideband high-frequency Pcal spread to become well-conditioned. The joint Fisher (`darm_callines.joint_fisher`) plus the simulated readout together state what each of those would require, rather than reporting a number the simulation does not support. ::: ## Remaining gaps On the coupled reduced-quad plant, the machinery tracks several parameters drifting at once, under a realistic random wander, within a Cramér–Rao bound, from a P&S-optimal designed cal-line drive, and the correlation matrix names the degeneracies rather than concealing them. What remains simplified: the random walk is a plain Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process (a Gaussian-process wander with a measured drift spectrum is the next step); the estimator is the two-step form (snapshot, then basis-fit) rather than the one-shot Lataire–Pintelon fit; the drift priors for all but `κ_C` are representative placeholders pending real per-parameter numbers; and `κ_M0`, `f_cc`, `τ` need the out-of-band / wideband lines noted above to join the tracked set. What this page establishes is the foundation: the question of whether a drift can be tracked gets a numeric answer, jointly, from an optimal drive — see `notes/darm-calibration-via-pns.md`.
